headline: Tallying a year of specimens

Records his game bag for the year

uncertain: The end of the tally is hard to read in the record, so the figures for squirrels, herons, trout and mackerel are unclear; only legible numbers are used. 'Batrachians' is rendered as amphibians.

headline: New Year's calls and three dear friends

tr_quotes.text: New York. Made about 20 calls. A particularly pleasant one on Annie Murray; she is a singularly sweet girl and one whom I wish I could serve.
is also a great favorite of mine - a pure, religious, bright girl well read and I think a true friend. Edith C. makes up my trio of Freundinnen.

uncertain: The record adds an editor's note to Fanny Smith's name, so the quote begins after it.

headline: Father's blessing, a spill, back to school

tr_quotes.text: The vacation has now come to a happy end, although it opened so gloomily; but I wish my dearest Father were better. Today he told me I had never caused him a moment's pain. I should be less than human if I ever had, for he is the best, wisest and most loving of men, the type of all that is noble, brave, wise + good.
great fun

headline: Taking stock of family and friends
summary: Missing home, Roosevelt fills a diary page with thoughts on his family and friends: Elliott has grown up, Jack Elliott is his closest friend after his brother, and Hal Minot, Will Blodgett, Minot Weld and Harry Chapin look like college friends in the making.

events.detail: Reflects in his diary on family, cousins and college friends

tr_quotes.text: Have naturally been thinking a good deal of home, especially of Father and of my darling Mother and sweet sisters, Elliott is a noble fellow, wonderfully grown up in every way.
I suppose, after him, Jack Elliott is my best friend, one who would do anything for me.

Of my college friends I should say, at present, that Hal Minot, Will Blodgett, Minot Weld and Harry Chapin, were likely to become friends, and very possibly George Pellew, Arthur Hooper and Charley Washburn.

uncertain: The record gives only the first name; Alfred is presumably cousin Alfred Roosevelt.

headline: Father laid to rest at Green-Wood
summary: After a short service at home and another at the church on 57th Street, the family crosses by ferry to Green-Wood Cemetery to bury Roosevelt's father. Roosevelt, shattered, pours out his grief in his diary and resolves to live as his father would have wished.

Writes a long diary entry of grief and resolve

tr_quotes.text: He has just been buried. I shall never forget these terrible three days; the hideous suspense of the ride on; the dull, inert Sorrow, during which I felt as if I had been stunned, or as if part of my life had been taken away;
He looked so calm and sweet.
With the help of my God, I will try to lead such a life as he would have wished.

headline: 'I owe everything to him'
summary: Roosevelt writes a tribute to his father in his diary, remembering his wisdom, his fairness and his unselfishness, and blaming himself for having done nothing for him.

events.detail: Diary tribute to his late father

tr_quotes.text: He was the most wise and loving father that ever lived: I owe everything to him. It is terrible to think I have never done anything for him, not even during his sickness.
He was so unselfish and was so continually making others happy that he was always happy himself, his 46 years of life were, excepting the last two months, very happy ones.

headline: Visiting Father's poor and old pupils

events.detail: Visits people his father aided
Reunites with his former mission school pupils

tr_quotes.text: He was as wise and good in public as in private life. He was a great personal worker among the poor; some of his old 'patients' whom I visited have been very touching about him.
By the way it is very pleasant to see my old Mission scholars again.

headline: Praise for Elliott and Bamie

events.detail: Diary praise for how the family nursed his father

tr_quotes.text: The family have all been simply wonderful during his illness, especially Elliott and Bamie.

headline: 'A father to the poor'
summary: Roosevelt struggles to accept that he will not see his father again and borrows a line from the Book of Job to describe him.

events.detail: Diary reflection on his father's memory

tr_quotes.text: It seems impossible to realize I shall never see him again: he is such a living memory.
Truly 'he was eyes to the blind, feet to the lame, and a father to the poor'.

uncertain: The record does not mark this as diary, but the words are in TR's voice and treated as his; the inner line echoes Job 29.

headline: Grateful for Uncle Jimmie's comfort

letters.topic: Thanks for a comforting condolence letter

tr_quotes.text: Every one has been very kind. I never shall forget Uncle Jimmie Gracie's sweet sympathy at the two times when I most needed it.
Your sweet letter cheered us up a great deal.

headline: Hardest on Mother and his sisters
summary: Roosevelt writes that the loss falls hardest on his mother and sisters, though it is terrible for all of them.

events.detail: Diary thoughts on the family's grief

tr_quotes.text: It is much worse for Mother and the girls than for me; but it is very terrible for us all.

headline: Like a hideous dream

events.detail: Brief diary entry on his grief

tr_quotes.text: Every now and then it seems to me like a hideous dream.

tr_quotes.text: I came back to Cambridge today. I am left about $8,000 a year; comfortable although not rich.

tr_quotes.text: Oh, my Father! what loving, living memories you have left in my head!
